body:
Meaning of Parallel Cinema

Parallel cinema, also associated with the Indian New Wave, refers to a movement that developed as an alternative to conventional commercial filmmaking. It gave particular importance to social realities, ordinary people and serious contemporary issues.

Its subjects frequently included rural poverty, unemployment, caste oppression, gender inequality, feudal exploitation and the experiences of marginalised communities.

The distinction between mainstream and parallel cinema is not absolute. Commercial films can address social problems, and parallel films can attract large audiences. The term describes a broad filmmaking movement and its priorities rather than a rigid legal classification.

Emergence of the Movement

The Bengali films of Satyajit Ray and Ritwik Ghatak during the 1950s provided important foundations for the development of parallel cinema. The movement became more prominent during the late 1960s and 1970s.

Film societies encouraged audiences to appreciate cinema from different regions and countries. Financial support from the Film Finance Corporation helped filmmakers undertake projects that commercial producers might have considered financially risky.

Important Filmmakers and Works

FilmmakerImportant workSocial significance
Satyajit RayPather Panchali (1955)Rural Bengali life and poverty
Ritwik GhatakMeghe Dhaka Tara (1960)Partition, displacement and family hardship
Mrinal SenBhuvan Shome (1969)Social hierarchy and bureaucracy
Shyam BenegalAnkur (1974)Rural exploitation and social inequality
Shyam BenegalManthan (1976)Dairy cooperatives and rural empowerment
Ketan MehtaBhavni Bhavai (1980)Caste oppression and untouchability

Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali was the first film of his Apu Trilogy. It received the Best Human Document award at the Cannes Film Festival in 1956 and helped bring Indian social realism to international attention.

Mrinal Sen's Bhuvan Shome is regarded as a landmark of the Indian New Wave that gained momentum in 1969.

Manthan: Gujarat's Dairy Cooperative Movement

Manthan, directed by Shyam Benegal in 1976, depicts the emergence of a dairy cooperative in a Gujarat village. It was inspired by the cooperative movement associated with Verghese Kurien and the transformation of India's dairy sector.

Approximately 500,000 dairy farmers contributed Rs. 2 each towards the making of the film. It is recognised as a pioneering example of crowdfunding in Indian cinema.

Its significance lies in presenting rural people as active participants in economic and social change rather than merely as beneficiaries of development.

Language and geographical setting

Manthan is a Hindi-language film about a movement rooted in Gujarat. A film set in Gujarat or inspired by Gujarati society is not necessarily a Gujarati-language film.

Regional Cinema Is Not the Same as Parallel Cinema

Regional cinema is a broad term for film industries associated with particular languages and cultural regions, such as Gujarati, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam cinema.

Parallel cinema, in contrast, refers to a filmmaking movement and its emphasis on social reality and alternatives to conventional commercial films.

The categories can overlap. Pather Panchali belongs to Bengali cinema and is an important precursor of the parallel cinema movement. Bhavni Bhavai belongs to Gujarati cinema and parallel cinema. Jesal Toral belongs to Gujarati popular cinema.

Prelims focus

  • Pather Panchali (1955): Satyajit Ray; Cannes recognition in 1956.
  • Meghe Dhaka Tara (1960): Ritwik Ghatak; Partition-related displacement.
  • Bhuvan Shome (1969): Mrinal Sen; landmark of the Indian New Wave.
  • Manthan (1976): Shyam Benegal; Gujarat dairy cooperatives.
  • Manthan was financed through contributions of Rs. 2 each from approximately 500,000 dairy farmers.
  • Trap: Regional cinema is not necessarily parallel cinema, and Manthan is a Hindi film despite its Gujarat setting.

[References: British Film Institute, Indian Parallel Cinema: 5 Essential Filmmakers from a Seismic Indian Cinema Revolution, 18 September 2024; Festival de Cannes, Pather Panchali film and award records; Film Heritage Foundation, Manthan (1976) historical account and Cannes Classics presentation, 2024; Directorate of Film Festivals, National Integration award retrospective; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Bhavni Bhavai. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The cooperative movement that inspired Manthan.

pictures.alt: Gujarati and parallel cinema overlap at Bhavni Bhavai; Manthan is Hindi with a Gujarat setting, and Bengali Pather Panchali is a parallel cinema precursor.

title: Parallel Cinema, Regional Cinema and Social Realism

body:
Cinema During the Freedom Struggle

During British colonial rule, Indian cultural expression was closely connected with the emergence of nationalism. Literature, theatre, music and cinema communicated ideas about Indian identity, freedom, dignity and resistance to injustice.

Early Indian filmmakers frequently used historical and mythological narratives that were familiar to audiences. Such stories could communicate ideas of courage, sacrifice and resistance without always referring directly to contemporary political events.

However, not every mythological or historical film was nationalist in purpose. Nationalist significance must be understood in relation to the particular film and its historical context.

Bhakta Vidur and Colonial Censorship

Bhakta Vidur (1921), directed by Kanjibhai Rathod, was an important example of indirect nationalist expression in early Indian cinema.

The character of Vidur, played by Dwarkadas Sampat, appeared in clothing associated with Mahatma Gandhi and was presented with Gandhian symbols such as the spinning wheel.

These references connected a traditional narrative with contemporary nationalist sentiment. British authorities prohibited the film in certain areas because of its political associations.

The episode illustrates how cinema could communicate nationalist ideas and how colonial authorities attempted to control politically influential cultural expression.

Cinema as an Instrument of Social Reform

Social reform involves efforts to overcome harmful practices, discrimination and inequalities within society. Cinema can contribute by portraying the experiences of affected people and encouraging public discussion about established social practices.

Unlike a formal law, a film cannot directly abolish a discriminatory practice. Its influence operates primarily through public awareness, empathy, discussion and changes in social attitudes.

Landmark Films Addressing Social Issues

FilmDirectorPrincipal issue
Achhut Kanya (1936)Franz OstenUntouchability and caste prejudice
Duniya Na Mane (1937)V. ShantaramForced and unequal marriage
Dharti Ke Lal (1946)K. A. AbbasFamine and rural deprivation
Do Bigha Zamin (1953)Bimal RoyAgrarian debt and urban migration
Bhavni Bhavai (1980)Ketan MehtaCaste discrimination and untouchability
HellaroAbhishek ShahPatriarchal restrictions and women's empowerment

Duniya Na Mane was the Hindi version of the Marathi film Kunku, directed by V. Shantaram in 1937. It should not be confused with the Gujarati film Kanku (1969), directed by Kantilal Rathod.

Cinema and the Experiences of Ordinary People

Indian films have also portrayed changes associated with industrialisation, urbanisation and migration. Films about rural indebtedness and workers migrating to cities brought attention to problems created by poverty and unequal economic opportunities.

For example, Do Bigha Zamin depicts the struggles of a poor cultivator threatened with the loss of his land. His migration to the city connects rural economic distress with the difficulties of urban working life.

National Integration and Cultural Diversity

After Independence, cinema continued to participate in discussions about citizenship, communal harmony, equality and national development. Films from different regions can help audiences understand communities and traditions beyond their immediate surroundings.

National integration through cinema does not require the disappearance of regional languages or cultural identities. Regional stories can communicate widely shared concerns about justice, dignity and equality while preserving their distinctive cultural character.

Prelims focus

  • Bhakta Vidur (1921): Kanjibhai Rathod; Gandhian symbolism and colonial censorship.
  • Achhut Kanya (1936): Franz Osten; untouchability.
  • Duniya Na Mane (1937): V. Shantaram; unequal marriage.
  • Dharti Ke Lal (1946): K. A. Abbas; Bengal famine.
  • Do Bigha Zamin (1953): Bimal Roy; agrarian distress.
  • Trap: Marathi Kunku (1937) and Gujarati Kanku (1969) are different films by different directors.

[References: Indian Institute of Mass Communication, Communicator, April-June 2017, discussion of Indian cinema and social reform, p. 51; Communicator, January-March 2019, section on films associated with Mahatma Gandhi; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Work, Life and Leisure, section 4.5, pp. 145-146; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, IPTA and Dharti Ke Lal; Press Information Bureau, 66th National Film Awards, 9 August 2019. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Cinema portrays social problems, encouraging awareness, empathy, discussion and possible attitude change, but cannot directly abolish discrimination.
pictures.caption: Cinema contributes to reform through awareness and public discussion.

title: Cinema, Indian Nationalism and Social Reform

body:
Cinema as a Medium of Cultural Identity

Cultural identity refers to the sense of belonging that people develop through shared languages, traditions, historical experiences, beliefs and cultural practices.

Cinema contributes to cultural identity by presenting these features through stories that audiences can recognise and understand. Regional cinema is particularly important because it expresses the experiences of communities through their own languages and cultural contexts.

Language and the Development of Regional Film Industries

The emergence of sound cinema in 1931 increased the importance of spoken language in Indian films. Dialogue, songs, local expressions and pronunciation enabled filmmakers to communicate more directly with particular linguistic communities.

This encouraged the development of film industries in numerous Indian languages. Gujarati cinema, beginning its sound-film history with Narsinh Mehta in 1932, became an important medium of Gujarati cultural expression.

Hindi cinema acquired a wide audience across different parts of India, while other language industries continued to develop their own distinctive identities. Indian cinema is consequently broader than Bollywood, which refers primarily to the Hindi-language film industry centred in Mumbai.

Indian cinema and Bollywood

Indian cinema encompasses films made across India's diverse linguistic and cultural traditions. Bollywood is a major part of Indian cinema, not a synonym for the entire Indian film industry.

Preservation and Transmission of Gujarati Culture

Gujarati cinema helps transmit regional culture by adapting literary works, portraying local social customs and presenting traditional music, dance and folklore.

Different films illustrate different aspects of Gujarati identity:

  • Narsinh Mehta: Gujarati devotional poetry and the Bhakti tradition.
  • Liludi Dharati: Gujarati literature and agrarian society.
  • Jesal Toral: regional folklore and moral transformation.
  • Bhavni Bhavai: folk theatre and criticism of caste discrimination.
  • Hellaro: Garba, rural Kutch and women's self-expression.

Cultural Exchange Across Regions

Films can reach audiences outside their original linguistic regions through subtitles, dubbing, adaptations and film festivals.

This allows a regional cultural expression to acquire national or international significance without losing its original identity. A Gujarati-language film receiving a national award is an example of regional creativity gaining wider recognition.

Similarly, a Hindi-language film such as Manthan can introduce audiences from different states to the experiences of Gujarat's dairy cooperative movement.

Cinema as Both a Reflection and an Influence on Society

Cinema reflects existing social conditions by portraying family relationships, occupations, aspirations, customs and conflicts. It can also influence society by popularising particular styles, expressions, social values and ways of understanding public issues.

These two relationships operate simultaneously. Social changes provide new subjects for films, while films can contribute to further changes in cultural attitudes.

The influence is not always positive. Cinema may challenge stereotypes and promote equality, but it may also reproduce prejudice or present misleading images of particular communities. Audiences do not necessarily respond to the same film in identical ways.

For this reason, cinema's social influence should be understood as a possibility shaped by content, audience interpretation and social circumstances, rather than an automatic effect.

Prelims focus

  • Sound cinema encouraged the growth of language-specific film industries.
  • Gujarati cinema draws upon Gujarati literature, folklore, devotional traditions and performing arts.
  • Hellaro connects Garba and rural Kutch with women's empowerment.
  • Regional identity and national integration can coexist.
  • Indian cinema includes multiple language industries; it is not limited to Bollywood.
  • Cinema can both reflect existing social values and influence changing attitudes.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Sociology, Standard 12, first edition 2017, Chapter 6, Mass Media and Society, pp. 57-65, particularly pp. 61-64; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Work, Life and Leisure, section 4.5, pp. 145-146; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarati cinema and individual film entries; Press Information Bureau, Hellaro recognition at the 66th National Film Awards and 50th IFFI, 2019. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026. The 2017 online textbook copy was consulted in place of the unreadable project Volume 37 scans.]

pictures.alt: Five Gujarati films represent devotional poetry, literature and agrarian society, folklore, folk theatre, and Garba and rural Kutch, sharing Gujarati cultural identity.
pictures.caption: Sources of Gujarati cultural expression in cinema.

pictures.alt: Society shapes cinema through social life; cinema can influence society through awareness, cultural exchange, changing attitudes and stereotypes.
pictures.caption: The two-way relationship between cinema and society.

title: Cinema, Language, Regional Identity and Cultural Change

body:
Why Film Certification Exists

Cinema can communicate powerful ideas to large audiences. The public exhibition of films therefore raises questions concerning artistic freedom, protection of children, public order and other legally recognised interests.

Indian law provides a system of examining and certifying films before their public exhibition. Certification determines whether a film is suitable for unrestricted viewing or requires particular audience restrictions or parental guidance.

Central Board of Film Certification

The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) is a statutory body functioning under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India.

It is constituted under Section 3 of the Cinematograph Act, 1952. Its chairperson and other members are appointed by the Central Government.

The institution was formerly known as the Central Board of Film Censors. Its present name came into use in 1983.

The CBFC is a statutory body because its authority originates in an Act of Parliament. It is not a constitutional body established directly by the Constitution.

Principal Functions of the CBFC

Under the Cinematograph Act, the Board can examine a film submitted for public exhibition and take a decision concerning its certification.

Its principal powers include:

  • Approving films for unrestricted public exhibition.
  • Approving films subject to parental guidance endorsements.
  • Restricting public exhibition to adults or specified audiences.
  • Requiring modifications or excisions before certification.
  • Refusing certification where legally justified.

The applicant must receive an opportunity to be heard before an adverse action under the examination provisions of the Act is taken.

Freedom of Speech and Expression

Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution guarantees citizens the right to freedom of speech and expression. Artistic expression through cinema falls within the protection of this freedom.

However, freedom of expression is not absolute. Article 19(2) permits the State to impose reasonable restrictions by law on specified constitutional grounds.

The constitutionally recognised grounds are:

  • Sovereignty and integrity of India.
  • Security of the State.
  • Friendly relations with foreign States.
  • Public order.
  • Decency or morality.
  • Contempt of court.
  • Defamation.
  • Incitement to an offence.

Section 5B of the Cinematograph Act establishes corresponding principles for film certification. The Board's authority must operate within the law and constitutional limitations; it does not possess unrestricted power to suppress artistic expression.

K. A. Abbas v. Union of India

In K. A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970), the Supreme Court examined the constitutional validity of prior film censorship and classification.

The Court recognised that films can have a distinctive and powerful impact on audiences. It upheld the constitutional permissibility of prior film censorship, provided that restrictions operate within the requirements of Article 19(2) and appropriate safeguards.

The judgment establishes that freedom of expression includes cinematic expression, but reasonable prior regulation of films is not automatically unconstitutional.

Appeals Against Certification Decisions

Section 5C of the Cinematograph Act permits an aggrieved applicant to challenge specified CBFC decisions, including refusal of certification, an unwanted restrictive classification or required modifications.

Following the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021, such an appeal lies before the High Court. It must ordinarily be filed within 30 days of the Board's order. The High Court may permit a further period of 30 days where sufficient cause prevented timely filing.

The earlier Film Certification Appellate Tribunal (FCAT) is no longer the statutory appellate forum.

Prelims focus

  • CBFC: Central Board of Film Certification.
  • Statutory basis: Section 3, Cinematograph Act, 1952.
  • Administrative ministry: Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
  • Article 19(1)(a): freedom of speech and expression; Article 19(2): reasonable restrictions.
  • K. A. Abbas case (1970): constitutional permissibility of prior film censorship subject to safeguards.
  • Section 5C: appeal to the High Court following the 2021 reforms.

[References: NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 2, Rights in the Indian Constitution, pp. 34-36; Constitution of India, Article 19; India Code, Cinematograph Act, 1952, Sections 3, 4, 5B and 5C, including amendments under the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021; Supreme Court of India, K. A. Abbas v. Union of India, judgment dated 24 September 1970, AIR 1971 SC 481; CBFC official website. Legal provisions consulted as of 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Constitutional freedoms and restrictions frame CBFC certification under the 1952 Act, with specified adverse decisions appealable to the High Court.
pictures.caption: Constitutional and statutory framework of film certification.

title: Central Board of Film Certification and Freedom of Expression
